newsitem.title: USA: Republicans step up attacks on INS.
newsitem.headline: Republicans step up attacks on INS.

text.p: House Republicans Wednesday stepped up their attacks on the Immigration and Naturalisation Service for granting U.S. citizenship to thousands of immigrants with criminal records last year.

"We are here to publicly examine what I can only describe as acts of shocking indifference and incompetence by an agency of the American government," Representative Dennis Hastert of Illinois said at a House Government Reform subcommittee hearing he chaired on the Citizenship USA programme.
The programme naturalised 1 million immigrants in the year before the 1996 U.S. elections.

"The failures of Citizenship USA are an insult to the hard-working and law-abiding immigrants who have truly earned this honour," said Representative Lamar Smith of Texas. "This situation once again demonstrates the lack of management responsibility and accountability at the INS."
Smith said 180,000 immigrants were naturalised without criminal background checks and another 71,000 who were granted citizenship had criminal records.

Some Republicans have said the White House pressured the INS to speed up the citizenship process so more aliens would be eligible to vote last November. The Washington Post reported Tuesday that the White House was under pressure from Hispanic groups to act.
INS Commissioner Doris Meissner said the programme was intended only to reduce a backlog of applications that had delayed processing from the usual six months to 2-4 years.
She said INS tried to process too many applications too quickly. "In hindsight, we see that our reach exceeded our grasp. We are doing everything we can to identify and correct our past errors."
INS is part of the Justice Department. Assistant Attorney General Stephen Colgate said the programme was being reviewed by the department and outside auditors KPMG Peat Marwick.
Colgate said he had been given authority by Attorney General Janet Reno to fix the problems. "She will do whatever it takes to get this corrected," he said.
Reno said Tuesday at another House hearing that steps would be taken to revoke citizenship for anyone who was improperly naturalised.

The National Council of La Raza, the nation's largest Hispanic group, said qualified immigrants should not have to wait years to become citizens. "Rather than be criticised for trying to get people through the naturalisation process in six months, the INS should be supported in its efforts to maintain this goal, while preserving the integrity of the process."
